name: Ekajuk
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kleiner, Werner & Renate Kleiner. 1968. The Ekajuk language of Nigeria: a grammatical description. Manuscript, 126 pp. (Achimota, Ghana: SIL). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 65106; copy of record downloaded from the web.archive.org capture 20240731113136 of the sil.org file URL.
catalog_locator: sec. 1.4.2 f) 'Stress and Tone', ms p. 7; sec. 1.4.2 'Tonal System', ms p. 4; sec. 3.1.2.2 'The Object is a Pronoun', ms p. 47
catalog_quote: [ms p. 7, sec. 1.4.2 f) Stress and Tone] Stress and tone are both lexical. Stress goes normally with the high tones. (see phon.) The object pronoun clitics, (see section 3.1.2.2.) the clitic -a (see section 3.2.4.) and the initial vowel of the items below have inherent stress whatever their tonal shape may be. [four tone-marked items:] area 'much' eji 'when' ana 'like that' owo 'then' The last three items show functional indications that they could have been noun clauses at some stage. (see section 3.2.) [ms p. 4, sec. 1.4.2 Tonal System] The tonal system is discussed in detail in the phonology. (see phon.) ... There are two tonal levels in Ekajuk, namely high (H) and low (L) plus a feature of downstep lowering automatically all high tones after low tones within certain grammatical units. ... Since tone (like stress) is a feature of the word and all combinations of L H and D are found, compressions of tones are common in one-syllable words. [ms p. 47, sec. 3.1.2.2] bo '3rd pers.pl.' is always a word. It is bo in all sets. It has its own peculiar tone pattern (HD). The other object pronouns have all inherent stress and high tone, irrespective of the set which occurs.

new_statements.relation_note: ekaj1238 is not in the catalog and had no existing statements, so this is a new statement rather than a comparison: tone language with a stress statement (stress lexical, normally accompanying high tone). Live sil.org URL answers with an automated-access block (two attempts, both 403); the file was archived copy (Internet Archive, 31 Jul 2024) of the same URL (HTTP 200, 8688016 bytes, 131 pdf pages).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ekajuk is a two-level tone language (H, L, plus automatic downstep, D). Stress is treated as a lexical, word-level property, not a positional one: it normally sits on the high-toned syllable(s) of the word. No initial/penult/final rule is given. A closed set of morphemes (the object-pronoun clitics -m -a -e -r -n, the clitic -a, and the initial vowel of area 'much', eji 'when', ana 'like that', owo 'then') carries inherent stress regardless of its tone. Details are deferred to the separate phonology ('see phon.' = Kleiner & Kleiner 1976, Preliminary phonological statement, microfiche only, not open).
new_statements.exceptions: Object pronoun clitics, the clitic -a, and the initial vowel of area 'much', eji 'when', ana 'like that', owo 'then' have inherent stress whatever their tonal shape; bo '3rd pl.' has its own HD tone pattern and is not in the inherently stressed set.
new_statements.identity_note: Kleiner & Kleiner 1968 describe the Ekajuk of Ntunop village (about 25 miles south of Ogoja) with assistants from Ntunop, Bansara and one other village, fieldwork April 1966 - July 1967; they state there is little diversity of speech within the Ekajuk clan (ms p. 1). Blench treats Ekajuk as one of the Bakor (Nkum sub-group) lects of Ekoid.

Supplementary, consistent with the compiler reading, not a new rule. Blench (the only work marked silent) was re-searched in full and is silent.
